Plus, we need to dispel the idea that "athlete = healthy." Even specifically "Olympic athlete = healthy." An athlete will often do things to their body which actively SACRIFICES health in order to obtain optimal performance. While most of the time, health and performance goals line up, whenever there is a dispute between the two, a competitive athlete will always choose to place performance over health, hands down.

A perfect example is a football player training versus playing. While training, most of what they do could be considered healthy. They'll be doing strength and conditioning work in a safe manner that minimizes risk of injury, and resting/recovering at proper intervals to improve their shape overall. If all they ever did was train, there would be no problem in calling what they do 100% healthy. BUT, when they step on the field to compete, things change. They no longer are trying to minimize injury risk; they're going all out to get the best performance possible (increasing the odds of hurting themselves), but they know they're potentially sacrificing their bodies for the game at these times. They do it because they're paid to, they love it, they're ultra-competitive, etc.

Enter the fat weightlifter... there's a reason some of these lifters are so fat. In certain lifts, the extra fat reduces the required range of motion needed to complete the lift, as well and improving their leverage so being fatter (to a point) gives them a competitive edge. Once again, you have an athlete sacrificing health (it's never healthy to be overweight/obese) in order to maximize performance. So while many times, a lot of what athletes do is healthy, you can't make the blanket statement that all athletes are "healthy."
